title: The Central Role of Noise in Evaluating Interventions That Use Test Scores to Rank Schools
research_question: Did Chile's P-900 program, which targeted resources and assistance to low-performing primary schools identified through their fourth-grade test scores, actually improve student achievement in treated schools? How large are the program's true effects on subsequent test score gains, and to what extent do conventional evaluations misattribute transitory test-score fluctuations to genuine program impacts?
data_description: The study uses school-level data from Chile's Ministry of Education, primarily fourth-grade achievement test scores in mathematics and language from the SIMCE (Sistema de Medición de la Calidad de la Educación) administered in 1988, 1990, and 1992, supplemented with earlier PER (Programa de Evaluación de Rendimiento) scores from 1984. The unit of observation is the school, with mean test scores constructed from the population of fourth-graders tested. Additional variables include fourth-grade enrollment, urban/rural classification, region (13 administrative regions), program participation status, and a Ministry-reported student socioeconomic status (SES) index (scaled 0–100) available from 1990 onward. The main analysis samples include 4,628 schools with 1988–1990 scores and 3,878 schools with 1988–1992 scores, with robustness samples restricted to urban schools having at least 15 fourth-grade students.
institutional_context: In 1990, Chile's government launched the 900 Schools Program (P-900), a compensatory intervention targeting roughly 900 of the country's lowest-performing publicly funded primary schools. The package included infrastructure repairs, instructional materials (textbooks, classroom libraries, cassette recorders, copy machines), weekly teacher training workshops in language and mathematics pedagogy, and after-school tutoring workshops for struggling third- and fourth-graders led by trained aides. Selection occurred in two stages: first, the Ministry of Education ranked schools by their combined 1988 fourth-grade mean test scores within each of Chile's 13 administrative regions and selected schools below region-specific cutoff scores; second, regional teams removed some schools from eligibility based on small size, rural/inaccessible location, or managerial problems to control program costs. Both publicly run schools and voucher-receiving private schools were eligible; elite tuition-charging private schools were not. Program assignment from 1990 remained in force through 1992.
